analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal equal pay enforcement and bans employers from using job applicants' salary history in hiring.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 220 House cosponsors in March 2025, the bill was referred to two committees and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The Paycheck Fairness Act would make it easier for workers to win pay discrimination cases: they could recover compensatory and sometimes punitive damages, sue as a class, and get attorney and expert fees paid. It would also ban employers from asking about or relying on a job applicant's past salary, fine employers for punishing workers who discuss their pay, require large employers to report pay data broken down by sex, race, and national origin, and fund negotiation-skills training. Small businesses exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act are exempt here too.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — especially women, who on average are paid less than men in similar work — gain stronger tools to challenge unequal pay: bigger possible damage awards, class-action lawsuits, protection for discussing wages, and a ban on salary-history practices that can lock in past discrimination. Job applicants gain because employers can no longer set pay based on what they earned before. The federal government gains better data to target investigations of pay discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and workers facing pay discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Workers who win pay discrimination cases could recover compensatory damages, and punitive damages if the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference, and such cases could be brought as class actions under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

The bill makes it unlawful for employers to fire or punish workers for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages, and bans contracts or waivers that prohibit employees from sharing pay information.

Employers would be barred from seeking or relying on a job applicant's wage history when hiring, with civil penalties of $5,000 for a first offense (up to $10,000 for repeat offenses) and up to $10,000 in special damages plus attorneys' fees for each affected applicant.

It tightens the employer's defense for paying people differently: any factor other than sex must be job-related, consistent with business necessity, account for the entire pay gap, and not be rooted in sex-based pay differences — and workers can defeat the defense by showing a less discriminatory alternative practice the employer refused to adopt.

Employers with 100 or more employees would have to report pay data broken down by sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC each year, which the agency must use to target investigations of pay discrimination charges.
The bill defines 'sex' under the Fair Labor Standards Act to include pregnancy, childbirth, sexual orientation, gender identity, and intersex traits, extending equal-pay protection to those workers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers. Businesses that lose pay discrimination cases would owe compensatory and potentially punitive damages plus expert fees, could face class actions, and would bear the cost of annual pay-data reporting for firms with 100 or more employees. Companies would face $5,000-$10,000 penalties per violation for seeking or using applicants' salary history, plus compliance costs for new posting and notice requirements. Small enterprises are exempt to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing lawsuits, penalties, and reporting

drawbacks.text: The bill significantly raises litigation exposure: employers losing pay cases owe compensatory damages, sometimes punitive damages, and expert fees, and the narrowed 'business necessity' defense makes it harder for employers to justify pay differences based on market rates or negotiation history.

Deeming workers at workplaces in the same county to be in the 'same establishment' could require comparable pay across locations with very different local labor markets and living costs, a burden employers would bear directly.
Employers with 100 or more employees would take on a new annual pay-data reporting requirement to the EEOC, a compliance cost the EEOC is told to weigh but not eliminate.
The training grants, research, and studies are funded by an open-ended authorization of 'such sums as may be necessary' rather than a set budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to a large group — workers whose pay may be unfairly discounted because of sex, pregnancy, sexual orientation, or gender identity — while the costs fall on employers in the form of litigation exposure, penalties, and reporting. The strongest honest objection is the design risk: the county-wide 'same establishment' rule and the narrowed business-necessity defense could penalize legitimate, market-driven pay differences and generate litigation even where no discrimination exists. The small-business exemption and the requirement that pay factors account for the entire gap temper the burden, and the salary-history ban preserves employers' ability to confirm prior pay after making an offer if the applicant volunteers it to argue for a higher wage. On balance the bill shifts real power and money from employers to workers, with the main cost being employer compliance and legal risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee has taken it up, so it has never come anywhere near a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 25, 2025, joined by 219 Democratic colleagues and one Republican as original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, with the Speaker to decide how jurisdiction would be divided.
Since that referral, the congressional record shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.
With Republicans holding the House majority, the 220 cosponsors are overwhelmingly minority-party members, so the bill has no obvious path to the floor in this Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that would face new damage awards, class actions, salary-history penalties, and pay-data reporting are better off because the bill has not moved; workers who might have used it to challenge unequal pay are no better off than before.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act and recruited 220 cosponsors, including every-name original cosponsors across the House Democratic caucus.

for.name: 219 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill support from a majority of the House — but only from members of the minority party.

for.name: Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: The sole Republican cosponsor, listed among the original cosponsors in the bill's introduction.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in March 2025 and has taken no recorded action — no hearing or markup — since.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in March 2025 and has taken no recorded action since.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; the record shows no vote or floor consideration of any kind.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed versions of the Paycheck Fairness Act as creating excessive litigation exposure and rigid pay rules for employers.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 219 Democrats to 1 Republican, and no vote was ever taken, so the bill's support was almost entirely from one party.

industries.note: These firms would owe annual pay data broken down by sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC, face compensatory and punitive damages and class actions in pay discrimination cases, and incur $5,000-$10,000 penalties per violation for using applicants' salary history. Their interest in avoiding these costs runs directly against workers seeking equal pay.

The Labor Department's contract compliance office would enforce the equal pay rules against federal contractors and collect compensation data from at least half of nonconstruction contractors each year, adding compliance and enforcement exposure for a defined subset of companies.

industries.industry: HR compliance and payroll data services
industries.note: The mandate for annual, disaggregated pay reporting by employers with 100 or more employees creates recurring reporting and compliance work that outside vendors would be paid to handle.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with no committee action more than a year into the Congress, under a House majority whose members are almost uniformly absent from the cosponsor list. In this situation the usual path is that the bill receives no markup or floor vote and quietly dies when the Congress ends in January 2027, unless a future Congress with different control revives it. A standalone equal-pay enforcement bill is unlikely to ride along on must-pass legislation.
